title: AI Email Drafts That Actually Sound Like You
summary: How Slashy learns your tone from sent history and drafts replies you can send with one keystroke, with the real acceptance curve from day 1 to day 30.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


Most AI email drafts read like a template because they're generated fresh each time, with no memory of how you actually write. Slashy runs an in-house memory system that learns your tone from sent history, and the drafts get measurably better over the first month: acceptance starts around 30% on day 1 and climbs past 80% by day 30.


Microsoft's[2025 Work Trend Index](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/worklab/work-trend-index/breaking-down-infinite-workday) put the average knowledge worker at 117 emails received a day, most skimmed in under 60 seconds. At that volume, the bottleneck isn't reading, it's replying in a voice that still sounds like you after the fortieth message. A generic AI draft can get the facts right and still read wrong, because it has no record of how you actually phrase a decline, a follow-up, or a quick yes. This post covers how Slashy's memory system closes that gap, what the acceptance curve looks like in practice, and where it stops short today.


## Why do AI-generated email drafts often sound wrong?


Most AI drafting tools generate a reply from the thread alone: the incoming message, maybe a system prompt describing a generic "professional tone." Nothing in that pipeline knows whether you write "Thanks!" or "thank you," whether you sign off with your name or just an initial, or how formal you get with a customer versus a co-founder. The draft is grammatically fine and personally wrong, which is why most people still rewrite half of it.


Slashy takes a different input: your own sent history. A memory agent continuously reads the emails you send, receive, and respond to, and builds a working model of your tone, the phrases you default to, who you talk to most, and how that changes by recipient. Drafting, triage, and scheduling all read from that same memory, so it isn't a one-time tone scan that goes stale.


## How long before the drafts actually sound like me?


This is the part worth being specific about instead of vague. Acceptance on AI-drafted replies, meaning the draft goes out with no edits or only a light touch, starts around 30% on day 1 and climbs to over 80% by day 30 as the memory system accumulates more of your sent history. The early drafts get the structure and facts right; you're still doing the voice work. By the end of the first month, most replies land in your tone on the first pass.


The ramp matters more than the day-one number. A tool that peaks on day one and stays flat is guessing well once. A tool that keeps climbing is actually learning.

## Can I send a draft without editing it?


Yes, and that's the point of the one-click send: a draft you trust goes out with a single keystroke instead of a full rewrite. When you do want to redirect a draft, the inline AI Assistant inside the composer lets you adjust the angle without leaving the message. You stay in control of what actually sends; the memory system just removes the blank-page step most of the time.

## Does it work across all my accounts, and on mobile?


Slashy supports Gmail and Google Workspace through Google OAuth, and multiple accounts run in one unified inbox with one-click switching. Outlook.com and Microsoft 365 are also supported, on web, desktop, and iOS. The memory model is per-account-aware, so a draft to your work address and a draft from a personal address both reflect how you actually write to that kind of recipient rather than blending into one generic voice.


On mobile, Slashy works over iMessage: you can ask it to draft a reply, triage urgent mail, or check your calendar by texting, and the drafts pull from the same memory layer as the desktop and iOS apps. A reply you approve from your phone reads the same as one you'd write at your desk.


## Is my sent email used to train shared AI models?


No. Slashy does not train models on your email, and enforces zero data retention with its AI providers. The memory that learns your voice is scoped to your own account, not pooled across users. Slashy is SOC 2 Type II and CASA Tier 2 certified, with AES-256 encryption at rest and TLS 1.2+ in transit.


## Where does this fall short today?


Two honest limits worth naming. First, the ramp means day-one drafts are still closer to a good template than a perfect match. If you need every send flawless immediately, budget the first week to sanity-check output the way you would with a new hire. Second, tone that shifts sharply and suddenly, a founder who changes register after a fundraise, a support lead who switches from casual to formal after a policy change, takes the memory system a few days to catch up to, not zero.


Start a trial and let the memory system watch a week of real inbox activity. The gap between day one and day thirty is the whole point.
